Part A — Examples of Conditional Statements

 
 
Part B — Conditional Statements
 
Question #1
 
```{r}
  
temp <- 33
if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot")
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}
 
``` 
Output:  [1] "Hot" 
Since 33 is 32 or higher, R prints "Hot".
 
 
 
Question #2
 
```{r}
  
age <- 17
if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age >= 13 & age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}
 
``` 
Output:  [1] "Teenager" 
17 falls between 13 and 19, so it prints "Teenager".
 
 
 
Question #3
 
```{r}
  
marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
result
``` 
 
Output:  [1] "Fail" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass" 
 ifelse()  checks every number at once and returns a vector of the same length.
 
 
 
Question #4
 
```{r}
  
x <- 10
if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}
``` 
 
Output:  [1] "A" 
R checks conditions from top to bottom. Since 10 > 5 is TRUE, it prints "A" and stops — it never reaches the second condition.
 
 
 
Question #5
 
Difference between  if  and  ifelse() :
 if  works on only one value at a time. Use it when you need to make a single decision.  ifelse()  works on every element in a vector at once, returning a vector of results. Use it when you need to process an entire column of data.
 
 
 
Part C — Importing the CSV File
 
Question #6
 
Import the file safely:
 
```{r}
  
# Set your working directory first if needed
# setwd("path/to/your/folder")

# Check if file exists before importing
if (file.exists("students_grades.csv")) {
  grades <- read.csv("students_grades.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  print("File imported successfully!")
} else {
  print("File not found — check your file path!")
}
``` 
 
Inspect the data:
 
```{r}
  
# First 6 rows
head(grades)

# Number of rows and columns
dim(grades)

# Column names and data types
str(grades)

# Basic statistics per column
summary(grades)

# Number of missing values per column
colSums(is.na(grades))
``` 
 
Answers:
 
- Rows & Columns: 15 rows, 7 columns
- Missing values: Midterm has exactly 1 missing value (Bea Navarro)
- Section type: Character
- Attendance range: Lowest = 70, Highest = 100
 
Check the data:
 
```{r}
  
nrow(grades)     # Should be 15
ncol(grades)     # Should be 7
sum(is.na(grades)) # Should be 1
 
 
``` 
 
Applying Conditional Statements
 
f.1 Compute Final Grade:
 
```{r}
  
# Final Grade = 30% Quiz + 30% Midterm + 40% Final
grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 0.30 * grades$Midterm + 0.40 * grades$Final
``` 
 
Note: Bea Navarro has a missing midterm, so her FinalGrade will show NA — that's expected.
 
f.2 Pass or Fail:
 
```{r}
  
# Check for NA first — NA comparisons give NA, not TRUE/FALSE
grades$Result <- ifelse(
  !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 75,
  "Passed",
  ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete", "Failed")
)
 
``` 
f.3 Grade Remarks:
 
```{r}
  
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent",
    ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",
      ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good",
        ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair", "Needs Improvement")
      )
    )
  )
)
 
``` 
f.4 Attendance Flag:
 
```{r}
  
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
 
``` 
f.5 Honors Candidates:
 
```{r}
  
grades$Honors <- ifelse(
  !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
  "Yes",
  "No"
)
``` 
 
f.6 Using a loop:
 
```{r}
  
# Initialize empty vector
Remarks2 <- character(nrow(grades))

# Loop through each row
for (i in 1:nrow(grades)) {
  if (is.na(grades$FinalGrade[i])) {
    Remarks2[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 90) {
    Remarks2[i] <- "Excellent"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 85) {
    Remarks2[i] <- "Very Good"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 80) {
    Remarks2[i] <- "Good"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 75) {
    Remarks2[i] <- "Fair"
  } else {
    Remarks2[i] <- "Needs Improvement"
  }
}
```
# Assign to data frame
grades$Remarks2 <- Remarks2
 
 
f.7 Why  if(grades$FinalGrade >= 75)  gives an error:
If you run  if(grades$FinalGrade >= 75)  directly, R warns you because the condition returns 15 values (one per row), but  if  expects only one TRUE or FALSE. The loop version works because it checks one row at a time with  grades$FinalGrade[i] .
 
f.8 Summarize Results:
 
```{r}
  
# Count of each result
table(grades$Result)
# Passed: 13, Failed: 1, Incomplete: 1

# At Risk students
table(grades$AttendanceFlag)
# At Risk: 4, OK: 11

# Honors candidates
table(grades$Honors)
# Yes: 4, No: 11
 
``` 
Check columns:
 
```{r}
  
ncol(grades)  # Should be 12 now
 
 
``` 
 
Part D — Exporting Results to .csv
 
Question #7
 
Export full processed table:
 
```{r}
  
write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
 
``` 
Export at-risk students:
 
```{r}
  
at_risk <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("At-risk list saved.")
} else {
  print("No at-risk students to save.")
}
 
``` 
Export honors list:
 
```{r}
  
honors <- grades[grades$Honors == "Yes", c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("Honors list saved.")
} else {
  print("No honors students to save.")
}
``` 
 
Verify exports:
 
```{r}
  
# Read back to confirm
check_processed <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv")
check_at_risk <- read.csv("at_risk_students.csv")
check_honors <- read.csv("honors_list.csv")

head(check_processed)
head(check_at_risk)
head(check_honors)
 
``` 
 
 
Question #8
 
- Missing midterm: Shows as an empty cell in the CSV; R reads it back as NA.
- Without  row.names = FALSE : R adds an extra first column with row numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) that you don't need in your final report. Always use  row.names = FALSE  for clean exports.
 
 
 
Question #9
 
Add Scholarship column:
 
```{r}
  
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
    ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial", "None")
  )
)
 
``` 
Select scholarship candidates:
 
```{r}
  
scholar_candidates <- grades[grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"),
                              c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance", "Scholarship")]
 
```
Export scholarship candidates:
 
```{r}
  
if (nrow(scholar_candidates) > 0) {
  write.csv(scholar_candidates, "scholarship_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print(paste(nrow(scholar_candidates), "candidates saved."))
} else {
  print("No scholarship candidates.")
}
 
``` 
Count each category:
 
```{r}
  
table(grades$Scholarship)
 
``` 
 
 
Question #10 — Short Answers
 
- Why check  is.na()  first? NA compared to any number gives NA, which neither  >=75  nor  <75  catches. Checking it first ensures missing scores are handled separately instead of causing errors.
- Order matters: If "Failed" came before "Incomplete", the NA rows would incorrectly be labeled "Failed" because NA comparisons don't return FALSE — you must handle missing values first.
-  ifelse()  vs  if : Use  ifelse()  when processing an entire column at once. Use  if ... else  when you need complex multi-step logic that varies per item or inside a loop.
- Why read exported files back? It confirms the file saved correctly and shows exactly how R will interpret it later — catches missing values, formatting issues, or accidental extra columns early.
```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
